questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a survivorship curve from a cohort
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the shape of a survivorship curve.
questions.stem: Sheet note 1: The projection shows a survivorship curve that drops steeply in the first year and then flattens out. What does that shape say about the population?

options.text: Most mortality happens early in life, so the few that survive the first year tend to live much longer
Most mortality happens late in life, so most individuals reach adulthood before dying
options.misconception: reads a steep early drop as late-life mortality

options.text: The population is growing rapidly, because a falling survivor curve means more births than deaths
options.misconception: confuses a survivor curve with a growth rate

options.text: The population is stable and replacing itself, because the curve eventually levels off at zero
options.misconception: treats a flattening curve as a stable population

questions.explanation: A curve that falls steeply early and then flattens is the concave shape of type I survivorship, with most deaths early in life. A survivor curve does not measure births, so it cannot give a growth rate or show replacement.
questions.hint: Look at where along the axis the drop happens.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Steps in building a life table
questions.learningObjective: Compute survivorship from a marked cohort.
questions.stem: Sheet note 2: A survey team follows a marked cohort of 200 animals; 150 are still alive at age 1 and 120 at age 2. Using the first step of a life table, what is survivorship at age 1?
questions.explanation: Survivorship is the fraction of the starting cohort still alive at an age: 150 / 200 = 0.75 at age 1. Dividing by the number alive at that age instead, or counting unmarked animals, changes the quantity.
questions.hint: Divide the survivors by the number at the start.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Fecundity against longevity as a trade-off
questions.learningObjective: Describe the trade-off between fecundity and longevity.
questions.stem: Sheet note 3: The projection compares a short-lived vole with a long-lived elephant, and asks what the trade-off usually means for reproduction.

options.text: Long-lived species reproduce more often, so each individual leaves many more offspring in a lifetime
options.misconception: assumes longevity always means more offspring per individual

options.text: Long-lived species usually reproduce later and less often, so lifetime output can be similar across species
Short-lived species reproduce only once, so their lifetime output is always much lower
options.misconception: assumes short-lived species breed just once

options.text: There is no trade-off, because lifetime offspring number is independent of how long an animal lives
options.misconception: denies any link between lifespan and reproduction

questions.explanation: The trade-off is that long-lived species mature later and invest less per year, so lifetime offspring numbers can be comparable even though the timing differs. Breeding once is not implied by lifespan.
questions.hint: Ask how early and how often each species breeds.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mark and recapture population estimate
questions.learningObjective: Apply the mark and recapture population estimator.
questions.stem: Sheet note 4: A survey marks 200 animals, releases them, and later catches 150 animals of which 30 are marked. Apply the mark and recapture estimate to find the population size.
questions.explanation: The mark and recapture estimate is M x C / R: 200 x 150 / 30 = 1000 animals. Adding the marked and unmarked catch, or dividing C by R alone, ignores the size of the marked sample.
questions.hint: Marked times caught, divided by recaptures.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a recapture estimate falls low
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a mark and recapture estimate can come out too small.
questions.stem: Sheet note 5: A marking survey releases 300 fish and later catches 60, of which 45 still carry tags, giving an estimate of only 400 fish in a lake that plainly holds more. What is the likeliest explanation?

options.text: The tagged fish were simply too few for the lake, so the estimate has an arithmetic error
options.misconception: blames sample size instead of tag loss

options.text: The catch of 60 was too small, so the estimate is low because of the small second sample
options.misconception: blames the second sample size

options.text: Tags were lost or the marked fish did not mix, so too many tagged fish appeared in the catch
Predators removed fish between the two samplings, which always lowers the estimate
options.misconception: assumes predation always lowers the estimate

questions.explanation: An estimate far below the true size happens when marked fish turn up in the catch too often, which tag loss or uneven mixing produces. Small samples widen the error rather than biasing it downward.
questions.hint: Ask why too many tagged fish appeared in the second catch.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Population size from successive removals
questions.learningObjective: Estimate a population from two successive removals.
questions.stem: Sheet note 6: Each sweep of the counting area removes the same fraction of the animals still present: the first sweep takes 120 and the second takes 80. Apply the successive removal formula to estimate the population.
questions.explanation: If each sweep removes the fraction p of what remains, then p = 1 - 80/120 = 1/3 and the population is 120 / (1/3) = 360 animals, which is S1 squared over S1 - S2. Adding the sweeps counts animals twice.
questions.hint: Find the fraction removed, then divide the first sweep by it.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Assumptions the removal method needs
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumption behind a constant fraction removed per sweep.
questions.stem: Sheet note 7: A diagram shows a pond swept three times, with the sweeps taking 200, 100 and 50 animals. Which assumption does this pattern rely on?

options.text: The pond is closed, so no animals enter or leave between the sweeps
options.misconception: lists closure as the only assumption of equal-fraction removal

options.text: Every animal is equally likely to be caught in each sweep, so the catches are independent
options.misconception: assumes independence of successive catches

options.text: The animals do not breed between the sweeps, so the total count stays fixed
options.misconception: confuses closedness with no breeding

options.text: Each sweep removes the same fraction of what remains, so the catches fall by a constant ratio

questions.explanation: The equal ratio between sweeps is the signal the method uses: the same fraction of the remaining animals is taken each time, letting the first catch stand for a fixed share of the total.
questions.hint: Compare each catch with the one before it.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the two growth-rate estimates differ
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of two growth-rate estimates for one area.
questions.stem: Sheet note 8: Design a comparison that would show why two estimates of a population's growth rate differ for the same survey area.

answer.exemplar: For the same survey area and the same season, run two independent lines of evidence: a mark and recapture census that gives a population size at two dates separated by several years, and a removal sweep that estimates the same size at a single date. Compute the finite rate of increase from the two censuses and the per-capita rate of increase from the removals, and record for each the quantities that could bias it, such as tag loss, emigration between dates, and animals missed in the sweep. Because the two methods sample the population differently, agreement between them narrows the list of explanations for any difference that remains.

questions.explanation: The comparison needs the same population measured by both methods, with the biasing factors recorded for each. Where the estimates differ, the gap must come from sampling, emigration, mark loss or closure.
questions.hint: Measure the same population two different ways.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a survivorship curve from a cohort
questions.learningObjective: Correct an inference about replacement drawn from a survivorship curve.
questions.stem: Sheet note 9: A draft says that a survivorship curve which levels off at the end proves the population is stable and replacing itself. Identify the flaw.

options.text: The curve shows how many survive, not how many are born, so it cannot establish replacement or stability
The curve levels off only if the population is measured with error, so the flattening is an artefact
options.misconception: treats a flat curve as a measurement artefact

options.text: The flaw is that survivorship curves must be drawn on a logarithmic scale to show the right shape
options.misconception: blames the choice of axis rather than the inference

options.text: The flaw is that a survivorship curve should be based on a static life table rather than a cohort
options.misconception: demands a static table instead of a cohort one

questions.explanation: A survivorship curve describes deaths within a cohort, so it holds no birth information and cannot show replacement. Axis choice, measurement error and table type affect how the curve is drawn, not what it proves.
questions.hint: A survivor curve records deaths, not births.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Steps in building a life table
questions.learningObjective: Identify the step needed between survival data and a reproductive rate.
questions.stem: Sheet note 10: A project asks which step must come between recording the survivors of a cohort and calculating its net reproductive rate.

options.text: Estimate the carrying capacity of the habitat, so that each age class can be scaled by space
options.misconception: inserts a capacity step into a life table

options.text: Measure age-specific fecundity, so that each age class can be paired with the offspring it produced
Fit a logistic curve to the cohort, so that the growth rate can be checked against the data
options.misconception: puts a logistic fit before the life table is complete

options.text: Convert all counts to percentages, because life tables may only be expressed as proportions
options.misconception: insists on proportions rather than counts

questions.explanation: A life table pairs survival with reproduction, so age-specific fecundity must be measured before any reproductive rate is calculated. Capacity, curve fitting and unit conversion are not table-building steps.
questions.hint: Survival and reproduction must be matched age by age.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Steps in building a life table
questions.learningObjective: Choose a field practice that protects the quality of a cohort life table.
questions.stem: Sheet note 11: A field team asks which practice keeps a cohort life table honest when the animals are hard to find at some ages.

options.text: Record the animals that are easiest to catch, so that the table reflects what is convenient
options.misconception: accepts convenience sampling as valid

options.text: Replace missing age classes with the average of the classes that were found
options.misconception: suggests interpolating missing classes silently

options.text: Mark the animals that were missed and note the effort spent, so that losses can be separated from deaths
Stop the study once too many age classes are missing, since no table can be built without them
options.misconception: treats partial data as unusable

questions.explanation: A life table is only as good as its detection record, so marking missed animals and logging effort separates animals not seen from animals that died. Convenience sampling and silent averaging distort the survival column.
questions.hint: Record what you failed to see as well as what you saw.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Fecundity against longevity as a trade-off
questions.learningObjective: Compare lifetime reproductive output for two life histories.
questions.stem: Sheet note 12: A sheet compares two species: one with a life span of 3 years and 8 offspring per year from age 2, another with a life span of 30 years and 1 offspring per year from age 10. What does the comparison show?

options.text: The short-lived species is far more successful, because it produces over 100 times more offspring in total
options.misconception: compares annual output instead of lifetime output

options.text: The long-lived species is far more successful, because it lives long enough to be counted as rare
options.misconception: judges success by longevity alone

options.text: Neither has an advantage, because both species produce exactly the same total number of offspring
options.misconception: claims identical lifetime output when the totals differ

options.text: Lifetime output is broadly similar, roughly 16 against 20, so the trade-off balances number against longevity

questions.explanation: Offspring per year times years of breeding gives about 16 for the short-lived species and about 20 for the long-lived one, so lifetime output is of the same order. Comparing annual output or longevity alone ignores the trade-off.
questions.hint: Multiply annual output by the years of breeding.

questions.stem: Sheet note 13: A tagging survey marks 500 birds, later captures 400 birds and finds 80 of them still tagged. Apply the mark and recapture formula to estimate the population.
questions.explanation: The estimate is marked times caught divided by marked recaptures: 500 x 400 / 80 = 2500 birds. Dividing the catch by the recaptures alone, or adding the two catches, does not estimate the population.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mark and recapture population estimate
questions.learningObjective: Explain why marked animals must mix before the second catch.
questions.stem: Sheet note 14: A note explains why the mark and recapture estimate assumes the marked animals mix back into the population before the second catch.

options.text: Because the estimate compares the marked share of the second catch with the marked share of the whole population
Because tagged animals grow larger and are easier to see, which improves the second catch
options.misconception: explains mixing by a visibility effect on tags

options.text: Because fish that carry tags travel further, so they spread across the survey area more quickly
options.misconception: explains mixing by tag-induced movement

options.text: Because tagging makes animals avoid each other, which spreads them out through the area
options.misconception: invites tag-induced behaviour change

questions.explanation: The estimator compares the marked share of the second catch with the marked share of the whole population, and those match only if the marked sample has mixed back in. Tag effects on size or movement are not the reason.
questions.hint: Ask whether the marked share of the catch reflects the population.

questions.topic: Why a recapture estimate falls low
questions.learningObjective: Quantify how far a recapture estimate falls below the true population.
questions.stem: Sheet note 15: A tagging survey marks 400 deer and later catches 200, of which 100 still carry tags, giving an estimate of 800 for a herd the ranch knows numbers 3000. What fraction of the true population is that estimate?
questions.explanation: The estimate is marked times caught over recaptures: 400 x 200 / 100 = 800 deer, which is 800 / 3000 = 0.267 of the true herd. Estimates that low usually mean marked animals appeared in the catch too often.
questions.hint: Divide the estimate by the known true size.

questions.topic: Population size from successive removals
questions.learningObjective: Read the pattern of successive catches in a removal diagram.
questions.stem: Sheet note 16: A diagram shows a sequence of four sweeps with arrows between them and catches of 150, 100, 67 and 45 animals. What is the diagram telling the cartographer to do?

options.text: To add every catch together, because each sweep removes different individuals from the population
options.misconception: assumes the sweeps are simply additive

options.text: To treat each sweep as a fraction of what remains, since the catches fall by a steady ratio
To use the largest catch alone, since it was taken when the animals were most numerous
options.misconception: takes the biggest catch as the population

options.text: To subtract each catch from the previous one, since the differences track the animals that left
options.misconception: misreads the differences as emigration

questions.explanation: The steady ratio between successive catches shows each sweep takes the same fraction of the animals still present, which lets the method convert catches into a population estimate. Adding or discarding later catches loses that.
questions.hint: Look for a constant ratio between the catches.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Assumptions the removal method needs
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of the closure assumption in removal sampling.
questions.stem: Sheet note 17: Design a survey that tests whether the successive removal method is safe to use on a mobile fish population.

answer.exemplar: Begin with a pilot sweep that closes the outlet of the counting area so that fish cannot leave or enter, and record the catch, the effort spent, and the water conditions, then repeat the sweeps under the same conditions with the outlet closed and again with it open. Compare the sequence of catches and the fraction of the population removed per sweep between the two treatments, and use the closed treatment to estimate the population and the open treatment to estimate how much immigration and emigration bias the method. Only if the two give similar fractions per sweep can the method be applied to the open area with confidence.

questions.explanation: The key assumption is that the sampled population is closed over the period, so a closed treatment gives a benchmark and an open treatment measures the bias from movement. Without that comparison the method can look reliable and be wrong.
questions.hint: Compare a closed area with one animals can enter.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the two growth-rate estimates differ
questions.learningObjective: Correct the treatment of two different growth-rate estimates as interchangeable.
questions.stem: Sheet note 18: A report gives a finite rate of increase from two censuses five years apart and a per-capita rate of increase from a single season, and treats the two numbers as interchangeable. Identify the flaw.

options.text: The flaw is that the finite rate of increase must be reported per year and not per five years
options.misconception: complains about the time unit of the census interval

options.text: The flaw is that a per-capita rate cannot be computed from births and deaths of tagged animals
options.misconception: claims tagged animals cannot yield survival rates

options.text: The two estimates come from different data and intervals, so they measure different things and need not match
The flaw is that the two numbers must be averaged before they can be compared with each other
options.misconception: proposes averaging rather than understanding

questions.explanation: A finite rate from two censuses spans five years of compounding, while a per-capita rate from one season covers only that season, so the gap is expected. They must be put on a common basis before comparison.
questions.hint: Check what period each estimate actually covers.

questions.topic: Reading a survivorship curve from a cohort
questions.learningObjective: Match a life history to the shape of its survivorship curve.
questions.stem: Sheet note 19: A cartographer's note asks which survivorship curve a species with heavy early mortality but long life for the few survivors would produce.

options.text: A convex curve that starts flat and then falls steeply, because mortality concentrates late in life
options.misconception: describes type II instead of type I survivorship

options.text: A straight diagonal line, because equal numbers die in every age interval of a cohort
options.misconception: describes type II instead of type I survivorship

options.text: A curve that falls steeply at first and then rises again, because survival improves with age
options.misconception: invents a rising tail on the survivorship curve

options.text: A curve that plunges early and then flattens, because most deaths come before maturity

questions.explanation: Heavy juvenile mortality with long life for the survivors gives the concave curve of type I survivorship, which drops steeply and then levels out. A straight diagonal is type II, and a rising tail does not occur.
questions.hint: Match the shape to where the deaths fall.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why life tables are built from cohorts.
questions.stem: Sheet note 20: A sheet asks why life tables are usually built from a cohort rather than from a single census year.

options.text: Because a cohort shows how the same individuals survive and reproduce as they age
Because a single census year cannot produce any usable mortality figures at all
options.misconception: dismisses static life tables as unusable

options.text: Because census data cannot be gathered for a whole population in a single season
options.misconception: claims census coverage is the obstacle

options.text: Because cohort tables avoid the need to mark or identify individual animals
options.misconception: suggests cohort tables avoid marking effort

questions.explanation: A cohort table follows one set of individuals through time, so survival at each age is measured for the same animals, linking mortality to reproduction. A single year's census gives one year's rates for a hypothetical cohort.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same animals are followed as they age.

questions.stem: Sheet note 21: A species first breeds at age 4 and produces 2 young per year until it dies at age 16. What is its lifetime output of young per individual?
questions.explanation: Lifetime output is offspring per year times breeding years: 2 young per year for 12 years gives 24 young per individual. Counting the years before first breeding, or changing the litter size, alters the total.

questions.topic: Fecundity against longevity as a trade-off
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a long-lived species spreads its reproduction.
questions.stem: Sheet note 22: A note asks how a longer-lived species usually spreads its reproduction across its lifetime.

options.text: All at once, in a single large litter produced early in life
options.misconception: assumes long-lived species front-load one huge litter

options.text: Spread thinly over many years, with fewer young each year and breeding starting late
Evenly but early, so the adults reproduce from their first year onwards
options.misconception: assumes long life implies early breeding

options.text: Not at all, because longer-lived species invest their resources in growth instead
options.misconception: claims long-lived species never reproduce

questions.explanation: The trade-off spreads risk: long-lived species start breeding later and produce fewer young per year, so a bad year costs them less. One large early litter is a short-lived species' pattern.
questions.hint: Ask when breeding starts and how many young per year.

options.text: The second catch of 100 was too small, which is why the estimate comes out low

The true population must have been 500, because the mark and recapture method never overestimates

questions.topic: Assumptions the removal method needs
questions.learningObjective: Identify how immigration breaks the removal method's closure assumption.
questions.stem: Sheet note 26: A diagram shows a stream section with a net at the downstream end and arrows showing fish moving in from the upstream side between sweeps. What problem does the diagram create for the method?

options.text: No problem, because the arrows show that fish are present, which is what the method requires
options.misconception: treats the presence of fish as evidence the method is sound

options.text: The problem is only that the net must be the same size in each sweep, which the diagram confirms
options.misconception: reduces the issue to equipment consistency

options.text: The problem is that fish moving downstream are counted twice, once in each sweep
options.misconception: claims double counting of downstream movers

options.text: Immigration breaks closure, so the sweeps keep sampling a population that is being replenished

questions.explanation: The method assumes a closed population between sweeps, and fish entering the block mean each sweep samples an augmented population, inflating the estimate. Presence of fish, net size and double counting are not the issue.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the two growth-rate estimates differ
questions.learningObjective: Design a field plan that isolates the causes of differing growth rates.
questions.stem: Sheet note 27: Design a field plan that would reveal why a population's growth rate from censuses differs from its growth rate from removals.

answer.exemplar: For one survey area, run the two methods in the same season: mark and release a known sample of the population, then remove a second sample by sweep, and repeat both at the same date six months later so that each method yields a population size at two dates and a rate of increase between them. Record everything that could separate the results, including the proportion of tags lost, the number of animals that moved in or out between dates, and how many animals each method failed to detect. Comparing the two rate estimates against those recorded sources of error shows which of them is large enough to explain the gap.

questions.explanation: Running both methods on the same population and the same dates puts the two rates on a common footing, so any gap must come from a recorded source of error. Without that alignment, timing, area and detection differences confound the comparison.
questions.hint: Use the same population and the same dates for both.

The flaw is that a survivorship curve for a hunted species must be plotted on a log scale

options.misconception: attributes the shape to the length of the study

options.text: The flaw is that carrying capacity applies to individual populations, not to whole species
options.misconception: mislabels the meaning of carrying capacity

questions.explanation: A survivorship curve describes deaths within a cohort and carries no information about how crowded the population is, so it cannot place the population relative to a capacity. Plotting scale and study length are not the issue.

questions.topic: Steps in building a life table

questions.stem: Sheet note 29: A note asks what a life table needs before the survival column l_x can be filled in.

A growth rate from a separate census of the same area in the same year

options.text: A set of age-specific fecundity values measured from the same animals
options.misconception: confuses fecundity data with survival data

questions.explanation: The survival column counts how many of the marked cohort are still alive at each age, so the cohort must be identifiable and its losses tracked. Capacity, growth rate and fecundity are later inputs.

questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that annual fecundity sets lifetime output.
questions.stem: Sheet note 30: A draft claims that a species which produces more offspring each year must also have a higher lifetime output of young. Identify the flaw.

options.text: The claim is sound, because lifetime output is just the annual litter size written down
options.misconception: accepts the annual figure as the lifetime total

options.text: The flaw is that lifetime output can only be measured in long-lived species, never in short ones
options.misconception: restricts lifetime measurement to long-lived species

options.text: Lifetime output depends on how many years the animal breeds as well as on the litter size
The flaw is that the annual litter size must be measured at the age of first breeding only
options.misconception: insists on a single measurement age

questions.explanation: Lifetime output is annual fecundity times years of breeding, so a species with a large litter but a short breeding life can match a slow-breeding one. Restricting measurement to one age changes the comparison.

options.text: Because animals must be marked twice, once before and once after the first catch
options.misconception: invents a second marking round

options.text: Because the population must be recounted at the same place to check for mark loss
options.misconception: treats a repeat count as the purpose of the second catch

options.text: Because the estimator compares the marked share of the later catch with the marked share of the whole population

options.text: Because the size of each later catch reveals the fraction of the population left, which scales the first catch up
Because removing animals makes the remaining ones easier to see on the next sweep
options.misconception: explains the estimate by improved detectability

options.text: Because every animal in the block is eventually caught, so the total is simply the sum
options.misconception: assumes complete capture of the population

options.text: Because removals disturb the habitat and drive animals out, so the count falls for known reasons
options.misconception: attributes the estimate to disturbance effects

questions.explanation: The ratio between successive catches gives the fraction of the population remaining, and that fraction scales the first catch up to the whole population. Easier detection and disturbance are not what makes the estimator work.

questions.topic: Fecundity against longevity as a trade-off
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of the fecundity and longevity trade-off.
questions.stem: Sheet note 37: Design a study that tests whether a population really trades fecundity against longevity.

answer.exemplar: Gather comparable life-history data for a set of populations along a body-size gradient, recording for each the age at first reproduction, the number of young produced per year, the length of the breeding life and the age at death, and calculate lifetime output for every population. Then test whether the populations with the highest annual fecundity really do have the shortest breeding lives, using a rank correlation rather than a single paired example, and check whether the pattern survives when populations of similar size are compared. Include at least one population that breaks the pattern, because a single exception is what shows whether a trade-off is a rule or a tendency.

questions.explanation: A trade-off is a tendency across populations, so it must be tested with several of similar size and analysed as a correlation between annual fecundity and breeding life, not as one paired example.
questions.hint: Compare many populations, not a single pair.

options.text: The two numbers are identical, because a finite rate is simply a per-capita rate written differently

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Population size from successive removals
questions.learningObjective: Design a successive removal survey for a lake margin.
questions.stem: Sheet note 47: Design a survey that estimates a population by successive removals in a shallow lake margin.

answer.exemplar: Work a defined margin block of the lake and close the block with seine nets on both sides, then make repeated sweeps with a smaller seine across the whole block, recording the number of animals in each sweep together with the effort used and the time of day. Repeat the sweeps until the catch falls below a fixed threshold, and calculate the fraction of the population taken per sweep from the ratio of consecutive catches. Continue the same protocol in a second block with an open boundary to measure how much fish moving in or out changes the estimate, and report the estimate with that measured bias attached to it.

questions.explanation: The protocol must establish a constant fraction removed per sweep, which needs the block enclosed and every catch recorded until numbers fall below a threshold. An open control block measures the bias from movement.
questions.hint: Enclose the block and keep sweeping until catches fall.

questions.topic: Assumptions the removal method needs
questions.learningObjective: Design a check on the constant fraction removed assumption.
questions.stem: Sheet note 48: Design a check that the successive removal method's assumption of a constant removal fraction holds in practice.

answer.exemplar: In a single block, run a long series of sweeps with a fixed method, log every catch in order, and then examine the sequence of catch sizes for a consistent proportional drop rather than a steady absolute decline, which would signal a changing fraction. Repeat the series under two different effort levels, such as overnight and daytime sweeps, so that the fraction removed per sweep can be compared between treatments, and record any animals that appear newly at the boundaries. Report the average fraction and its spread across sweeps and treatments, since a method that relies on a constant fraction is only as good as that constancy.

questions.explanation: The assumption is testable from the series of catches: a constant fraction removed produces a geometric decline, and the spread of estimated fractions shows how reliable that is. Varying effort tests whether the fraction depends on method.
questions.hint: Look for a constant ratio in the sequence of catches.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the two growth-rate estimates differ
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison that documents why two growth rates disagree.
questions.stem: Sheet note 57: Design a comparison that documents why a survey's two growth-rate estimates disagree.

answer.exemplar: Take a single study area and produce three numbers from it: a population size at two dates from repeated censuses, a population size at one date from a removal sweep, and the births and deaths recorded over the same twelve months. Convert each source into a rate of increase on a common one-year basis, so the censuses are turned into a finite rate that can be compared with the per-capita rate from births and deaths. Alongside the numbers, log the sources of bias for each method, such as tags lost between the dates, animals entering or leaving the area, and those missed in the sweep, so that the size of each contribution to the disagreement can be reported.

questions.explanation: Putting all three measurements on one time basis makes the comparison meaningful, and logging biasing factors with each rate shows which is large enough to explain the disagreement. Without common units the numbers only sit side by side.
questions.hint: Convert every estimate to the same time basis.

questions.topic: Reading a survivorship curve from a cohort
questions.learningObjective: Correct an inference about growth drawn from a survivorship curve.
questions.stem: Sheet note 58: A draft claims that because a survivorship curve is concave, the population must be growing exponentially. Identify the flaw.

options.text: The flaw is that survivorship curves are only meaningful for closed populations with no migration
options.misconception: blames population closure for the inference

options.text: A survivorship curve describes deaths within a cohort, so its shape says nothing about how the population grows
The flaw is that concave curves describe declining populations rather than growing ones
options.misconception: reads curve shape as a growth signature

options.text: The flaw is that the curve should be drawn against the number of births rather than the age scale
options.misconception: suggests a different axis removes the problem

questions.explanation: The shape of a survivorship curve is the pattern of deaths within a cohort, and births and total size never appear in it. Whether a population grows depends on the birth rate and age structure.
questions.hint: A survivor curve records deaths, not births.

questions.topic: Steps in building a life table
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a life table records both survival and young produced.
questions.stem: Sheet note 59: A sheet asks why a life table records both the number alive at each age and the number of young produced at each age.

options.text: Because the survivor column alone cannot show whether the population is replacing itself
options.misconception: credits the survivor column with the wrong purpose

options.text: Because counting young is a quick way of estimating the number of adults in the cohort
options.misconception: treats a fecundity count as an adult count

options.text: Because survival and reproduction must be paired by age before any growth rate can be estimated
Because the young column makes the table easier to read when the rows are printed
options.misconception: gives a presentational reason for a data column

questions.explanation: A growth rate needs to know how many reach breeding age and how many daughters each produces, matched age by age. Neither column substitutes for the other, and the second is not for printing.
questions.hint: Survival and reproduction must be joined by age.

questions.topic: Fecundity against longevity as a trade-off
questions.learningObjective: Compute lifetime reproductive output from a life history.
questions.stem: Sheet note 60: A species first breeds at age 5 and produces 3 young per year until it dies at age 15. What is its lifetime output of young per individual?
questions.explanation: Lifetime output is offspring per year times breeding years: 3 young per year for 10 years gives 30 young per individual. Counting the years before breeding changes the total compared.
questions.hint: Multiply the litter size by the years of breeding.
